title: Naming Jazz and Afro-American music
summary: Ramirez says the Establishment is reluctant to name Black music and prefers "Afro-American" to "Black"; White and non-White.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It's like so many people object to the word Jazz, but you're stuck with it, aren't you.

True. And in the act of searching for some new advances, it seems to me the Establishment somewhere along the line is reluctant to give it any identification, simply because of the nature where the history of it begins, which is just... It's just Black folk in America. I mean,
White people have their own thing, I suppose, so far as Country music and that is concerned...
Well, Country Music is now...the term isn't derogatory, is it.
No. Well, Black people are just as affected by this so-called American Country Music as Whites are.
You can see in the beginning that idea of Jazz and (?) music... Jazz was an appropriate word for it.
It doesn't... I remember you saying that Duke avoided the word "Jazz."

Oh, he did. But the sort of ribald country songs that they say that Bach and people like that used in their music, and then in the course of time... Folk music is often, you know, just kind of dirty songs almost. But they get incorporated in symphonic music!

But I would much rather say... Like, instead of saying "Negro" this, I would much rather say the axioms (as far as axioms go) say "Afro-American beginning," "Afro-American style." I don't like the expression Black off-handedly, because I mean... You know, I have a color television, you know.
I always say that if I am going to make a difference between that... Since Caucasian predominates, I
would say White and non-White. Which includes the Indian and the Oriental as (?), you know.
